stone-town.hook: The UNESCO-listed old town an hour and a quarter south of Kendwa: market, memorial, night food, rooftops.
stone-town.why: Stone Town was inscribed by UNESCO in 2000 as a Swahili trading town built of coral stone, and almost everything on a north-coast menu passed through its port first. A single day can follow the food: Darajani market, opened in 1904, in the morning; the cathedral built on the last open slave market at midday; the Forodhani gardens when the grills light at dusk; then a rooftop dinner above the town before the drive back north.
facts: Stone Town of Zanzibar was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2000 (record tag; UNESCO).
Darajani Market's main building was inaugurated in August 1904 under Sultan Ali bin Hamud (Wikipedia, Archnet).
The House of Wonders' front partially collapsed on 25 December 2020 and the building is still under Oman-funded restoration (Wikipedia; Oman Observer).
Sauti za Busara festival moved from the Old Fort to Mnazi Mmoja Grounds for its 2026 edition, 6-8 February 2026 (The Citizen).

forodhani.hook: Stone Town's seafront park, rebuilt in 2009, where food stalls set up every evening at sunset.
forodhani.why: The name means customs, after the customs house that stood here, and the gardens were called Jubilee Gardens until the 1964 revolution. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture rebuilt the park, seawall and lighting, finishing in July 2009. Each evening the grills and fryers go up in front of the Old Fort: Zanzibar pizza folded and fried to order, urojo ladled over bhajia and crisps, sugar cane pressed with lime and ginger.
facts: 'Forodhani' means customs; the gardens stand near the original customs house (Archnet).
The gardens were called Jubilee Gardens until the 1964 revolution (Archnet).
A white arabesque arch near the sea was erected in 1956 for Princess Margaret's visit (Archnet).
The Aga Khan Trust for Culture completed the park's revitalisation in July 2009, with the Revolutionary Government of Zanzibar (AKDN press release).
The night market sells Zanzibar pizza, urojo (mango-tamarind soup with bhajia and cassava crisps) and grilled seafood (AFAR; The East African).

emerson-hurumzi.hook: A Stone Town rooftop dinner on floor cushions: US$45 for three courses, taarab musicians most evenings.
emerson-hurumzi.why: Emerson on Hurumzi is three old merchants' houses joined together, one of them once owned by Zanzibar's archbishop, and its tea house is billed as the highest rooftop restaurant in Stone Town. lukmaan.hook: A Stone Town canteen near the old slave market: point at the trays on the counter, and they plate it up.
lukmaan.why: There is no menu at Lukmaan. You go to the counter, look at what is in the trays that day, and point: biryani, pilau, fried fish, coconut curries, cassava, spinach, fresh naan. Plates come out large and cheap, eaten at shared tables among people who live in Stone Town rather than visit it. It sits on Mkunazini Street a few minutes' walk from Christ Church, which makes it the obvious lunch after the slave-market memorial.

darajani.hook: Stone Town's main food market since 1904: spice by the scoop, fish on slabs, fruit and grain.
darajani.why: The tin-roofed hall on Market Street was opened in August 1904 for Sultan Ali bin Hamud, designed by the British architect J.H. Sinclair, and Stone Town still calls it Marikiti Kuu, the main market. It sells what households need: cloves, cardamom and cinnamon loose by weight, rice and grain, fruit, meat, and the morning's fish in a hall you find by its smell. Buy spice here by the scoop rather than boxed for the airport.
facts: The main market building was built in 1904 by Bomanjee Maneckjee for Sultan Ali bin Hamud (Wikipedia).
It was designed by British architect J.H. Sinclair and inaugurated in August 1904 (Wikipedia).
It is also known as Estella Market and, informally, Marikiti Kuu, 'main market' (Wikipedia).
It is mainly a food market, with seafood, meat, fruit, grain and spice sections (Wikipedia).

mnemba.evidence: Natural site with authoritative current descriptions: Zanzibar's revised marine conservation fees (in force from 1 Sept 2025, reported by The Citizen and Tourism Update) and &Beyond's current Mnemba reef-restoration pages. Snorkel trips widely bookable for 2026-27.

sources.label: The Citizen, Zanzibar revises marine conservation entry fees

corrections: Fee: old says US$10 per person. Since 1 Sept 2025 there are two regimes: the wider Mnemba Island Marine Conservation Area (MIMCA) charges non-EAC adults US$10 per day (children 5-15 US$5), but the Mnemba Island Marine Special Area kept its fee of US$25 per non-EAC adult and US$10 per child. Write 'a conservation fee of US$10-25 depending on zone - check what the operator includes' (The Citizen; Tourism Update).

Reef restoration: &Beyond names it the Reef Stars project using the MARRS hexagonal frames, started in response to the February 2024 mass bleaching; Oceans Without Borders was founded by &Beyond and Wild Impact (formerly Africa Foundation) in 2018. Old text's 'coral-reef restoration project' is correct; add the name.
'Turtles are common' and 'best snorkelling reachable from the north tip' are not confirmed by an authoritative source; keep as the guide's view.
mnemba.hook: A private atoll off Unguja's north-east coast, ringed by a marine conservation area you reach by boat.
mnemba.why: The island is private, run as an &Beyond lodge, and day boats cannot land, so the trip is entirely about the water around it, which is a protected marine area with its own entry fee. After the February 2024 global bleaching hit the reef, &Beyond and Wild Impact began fixing hexagonal steel 'reef stars', built by people from nearby villages, onto the coral rubble and planting them with nursery-grown fragments.
facts: Since 1 Sept 2025, MIMCA entry is US$10 per non-EAC adult per day and US$5 per child 5-15 (The Citizen).
The Mnemba Island Marine Special Area kept a US$25 per non-EAC adult and US$10 per child fee (Tourism Update; The Citizen).
Oceans Without Borders was founded by &Beyond and Wild Impact (formerly Africa Foundation) in 2018 (&Beyond).
The Reef Stars project uses the MARRS hexagonal frames, built locally, to stabilise coral rubble after the February 2024 bleaching (&Beyond).
Shared snorkel trips to Mnemba are quoted from about US$30-45 per person for 2027 (Safarifind, operator aggregator).

leven-bank.hook: A submerged mountain in the Pemba Channel north of Nungwi, an advanced drift dive in strong current.
leven-bank.why: Leven Bank is a seamount out in the Pemba Channel whose top sits about fourteen metres down, and divers with the right qualifications go to around fifty. The current across it is strong enough that the north-tip centres pick the day by conditions, not by the calendar, and take only experienced divers. Those who go come back describing large groupers, moray eels, tuna and barracuda, and sometimes rays or dolphins.
facts: Leven Bank is a submerged mountain in the Pemba Channel north of Nungwi (Tanzania Specialist).
The summit is about 14 m below the surface; experienced divers go to up to about 50 m (Tanzania Specialist).
Strong currents make it suitable only for experienced divers in good conditions (Tanzania Specialist).
Marine life includes large groupers, moray eels, tuna and barracuda, with occasional rays and dolphins (Tanzania Specialist).
Centres in Nungwi and Kendwa (East Africa Diving, Team Aqua, One Ocean, Scuba Do) list it among their sites (dive.site; Holafly).

kizimbani.hook: A spice farm in central Unguja where you see cloves, nutmeg, vanilla and cinnamon on the plant.
kizimbani.why: The clove is an unopened flower bud, and at Kizimbani you see it on the tree before it is dried and sold by the scoop in Stone Town. The guided walk goes plant by plant: nutmeg split to show the red mace around the seed, vanilla vine, cinnamon bark and leaf, lemongrass, pepper, with fruit to taste on the way. The dry months from June to October are the best time to go.

Most spice tours there are run by local operators; the farm functions largely as a visitor attraction (Wikipedia).
Tours show cloves, cinnamon, vanilla, nutmeg, pepper, ginger and lemongrass, with fruit and spice tastings (Zanzibar tourism listings; operator pages).
Guided Kizimbani tours last about 3-4 hours (Magpie listing).
June to October, the dry season, is cited as the best time for a spice tour (Duma Explorer 2026).

old-fort.hook: The Omani fort on Stone Town's seafront, its courtyard free to enter and its amphitheatre used for shows.
old-fort.why: The Omani rulers of Zanzibar built the fort on the site of an earlier Portuguese church, and it still stands at the head of the seafront beside Forodhani. In 1994 part of the courtyard became an open-air amphitheatre, which for 22 years hosted the Sauti za Busara music festival until it outgrew the walls and moved to Mnazi Mmoja in 2026. The courtyard is free and opens straight onto Forodhani.
facts: The Old Fort stands on the seafront next to the House of Wonders and Forodhani (Archnet).
Part of the fort became an open-air amphitheatre in 1994 (guide summaries).
Courtyard entry is free; listings give daily 08:00-18:00 (AAA/guide listings, not official).
Sauti za Busara was held at the Old Fort for over 22 years before moving to Mnazi Mmoja Grounds for 2026 (The Citizen).

anglican-cathedral.hook: The cathedral on the site of Zanzibar's last open slave market, with holding chambers and a memorial.
anglican-cathedral.why: Sultan Barghash closed the public slave market under British pressure in 1873, and missionaries built Christ Church on the same ground, opening it in 1879. A heritage centre at the gate, opened in 2016, tells the trade's story before you reach the cramped holding chambers. Outside, five figures by the Swedish artist Clara Sörnäs, installed in 1998, stand in a pit, chained at the neck.
facts: The public slave market closed after Sultan Barghash bin Said signed a treaty in 1873 (Slavery Monuments).
Christ Church Cathedral was built on the market site and inaugurated in 1879 (Slavery Monuments summary).
A slave-trade heritage centre at the cathedral opened in 2016 (Anglican News).
The 'Memory for the Slaves' sculpture by Clara Sörnäs was installed on 2 May 1998: five figures in a pit, four chained at the neck (Slavery Monuments).
Entry, covering exhibit, chambers and cathedral, is quoted at US$5-10 in guides; pay cash (guide summaries).

house-of-wonders.hook: The sultan's 1883 palace on Stone Town's seafront, partly collapsed in 2020 and still closed for restoration.
house-of-wonders.why: Built in 1883 as a sultan's palace, it was the first building in Zanzibar with electricity and a lift. Oman had already agreed to pay for a restoration when the front corner fell on Christmas Day 2020, with loss of life. Oman is funding the rebuilding, which includes strengthening 240 columns and terraces, and the two governments have agreed it will reopen as a museum. For now you see it from Forodhani.
facts: The front, north-west corner, partially collapsed on 25 December 2020 with loss of life (Wikipedia; Lidar News).
Oman agreed to fund the restoration at RO 5,931,770, including strengthening the building's 240 columns and terraces (Oman Observer).
The regeneration programme began in May 2018 and is programme-managed by Zamani (Lidar News/excursion summaries).
Oman and Zanzibar signed a foundation document for museum use of the restored building (Oman Observer).
As of October 2025 the building was still a hollow shell under works; no reopening date has been announced (search summaries of visitor reports).

freddie-mercury.hook: A small museum on Kenyatta Road, opened in 2019, on Farrokh Bulsara's Zanzibar childhood.
freddie-mercury.why: Javed Jafferji named the Shangani building Mercury House in 2002 and spent fifteen years turning it into a museum, which opened in November 2019 with photographs loaned by Queen Productions. It covers Farrokh Bulsara's Zoroastrian Parsi family, his childhood in a British-protected sultanate and his schooling in India before London. The family lived here in the 1940s. Visits take about half an hour, in air conditioning.
facts: The Freddie Mercury Museum was officially inaugurated on 24 November 2019 (Queen Online/press).
It is at 57 Kenyatta Road, Shangani, and partnered with Queen Productions Ltd, which loaned photographs (press coverage).
Co-founders are Javed Jafferji and Andrea Boero; Jafferji named the building Mercury House in 2002 (CNN; Homegrown).

The museum covers his Zoroastrian roots, Zanzibar childhood and schooling in India (Queen Online summary).

flame-tree.hook: Garden cottages at the quiet north-west end of Nungwi beach, with restaurants open onto the sand.
flame-tree.why: Flame Tree is a small hotel of individually styled cottages, with Zanzibari beds and Swahili wood furniture, set in a garden of coconut palms, frangipani and the red-flowering flame trees it is named for. nungwi-village.hook: Nungwi's small shops and fruit sellers: rice, oil, eggs, limes, charcoal, and fish from the landing.
nungwi-village.why: Cooking at the north tip means buying the way the village does. Small shops through Nungwi sell rice, flour, oil, eggs, onions, tomatoes, limes, chillies and charcoal, with a couple of mini-markets on the square. Fruit comes from street sellers, fish and octopus from the boats at the landing in the morning. Imported wine, cheese and bulk spice mean a trip to Stone Town, a full day there and back.
facts: A travel account reports a couple of small supermarkets and a pharmacy on the Nungwi square (svudapodji.com, 2022).
Mbweni Super Market, stocking imported goods, is in the Zanzibar Town area, not Nungwi (Wanderlog listing).
Nungwi is a fishing village at the northern tip of Unguja (Wikipedia).

combo-1990.hook: A small Nungwi village restaurant serving Swahili dishes as a spread of small plates.
combo-1990.why: Combo 1990 sits in the middle of Nungwi village rather than on the beach, and its format is the lesson: a spread of small plates from the day's pots, so you taste several Swahili dishes in one sitting rather than committing to one. A French writer on Nungwi singled it out for exactly this, noting the plates cost a few euros. Ugali, rice and chapati come alongside.

tamtam.hook: A local Zanzibari restaurant a street back from Nungwi beach, cooking rice, fish and greens.

jf-kili.hook: A Nungwi coffee house and coffee truck pouring beans from the owners' farm below Kilimanjaro.
jf-kili.why: The owners are Tanzanian and grow the coffee themselves on a farm under Kilimanjaro, then sell it at the other end of the country on a beach where most coffee arrives in a tin. There are two places to drink it in Nungwi: the coffee house on the main road opposite Hanoi House, and a truck with a few tables on the big square next to MJ's. Waffles and cakes as well.
